title: The Screen Experiment
goal: Your kid turns screen rules into an experiment. They guess their daily screen time and check it against the device's own report, find the point where a session turns, pick one rule and predict what it will change, test it for a week, then help write the family plan from what their own evidence showed.
need: Each device's screen-time report (Screen Time on Apple, Digital Wellbeing or Family Link on Android). Most phones keep one already; if yours is off, turn it on a few days before you start
A notebook for each person's guesses and notes
One ordinary week for the test

academics.subject: Health
academics.text: how screens affect mood and sleep

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Your job is to run the experiment with them, not to win it. Guess your own number first, test a rule on your own phone, and when a result surprises you, say so out loud. The plan only works if the evidence is allowed to change your mind too.

plan.what: Guess, check the reports and find the turn (Steps 1 and 2).
Pick one rule, predict, then run the test (Steps 3 and 4).
Write the plan from the evidence and sign it (Step 5).

troubleshoot.q: The report shows far more than anyone guessed
troubleshoot.a: That's the starting data, not a verdict. Read the numbers without a lecture, yours included, and move on to finding the turn.

troubleshoot.q: They rate every check a 5 so the screen stays on
troubleshoot.a: Do the checks out loud together, and add a note they can't fudge, like how long it takes to get going on something else after.
Different results, different rules. Lay their notes side by side and let them see why one rule fits one kid and not the other.

troubleshoot.q: Most screen time is the TV or a shared tablet
troubleshoot.a: No report covers that. For a few days, keep a tally on the fridge each time it goes on and off, and use that as your real number.

lesson.text: Most people, grown-ups too, guess their screen time wrong, and the moment a session turns is hard to feel from inside it. Turning one rule into a test with a prediction gives the family a result everyone saw, so the plan rests on evidence instead of 'because I said so'.
lesson.before: 'I'm barely on it. Can I have five more minutes?'

model.line: 2 hours 10 minutes a day, 70 minutes more than the guess.
Mood checks every 15 minutes read 5, 5, 4, 2. It turned between 45 and 60 minutes.
A 45-minute timer. The number at the end went from mostly 2s to mostly 4s.

lesson.modelNote: 'Barely on it' was a feeling. The report gave a real number, the mood checks showed where the session turned, and the 45-minute limit came from the kid's own checks instead of a rule handed down.

steps.title: Guess, then check
steps.why: Almost everyone guesses their screen time wrong. Writing the guess down first is what makes the real number land.
steps.kid: Your kid writes a guess for their daily screen time, then opens the device's own report with you, using the Guess and check card in the Screen Experiment Toolkit at the end of the guide. They work out the gap in minutes.
steps.you: Guess yours too, write it down before you look, and read your real number out loud, even if it's not flattering.
ask: What did you guess, and what did the report say?
Which app took more time than you thought?
steps.tip: Count everything the report shows, AI chats and video calls included. It's all screen time.

levels.explore: Show with your arms how long you think you were on screens today, then see the real number with a parent.
levels.develop: Guess your daily average, check it on the report, and work out how far off you were in minutes.
levels.extend: Guess for every person in the family, then draw a bar chart of guesses next to real numbers and see who guessed low and who guessed high.

steps.title: Find the turn
steps.why: Screen time rarely goes bad all at once. There's usually a point where it turns, and you can't feel it from inside without checking.
steps.kid: During a normal screen session, a timer rings every 15 minutes and your kid gives a quick number from 1 to 5, using the Mood check card. They do this for three or four sessions, then look for the point where the number drops.
steps.you: Set the timer and ask for the number out loud, with no comment on the number. Run the same checks on one of your own phone sessions.
ask: When did your number start to drop?
Is it the same spot every time?
steps.tip: Keep each check under ten seconds. A long pause changes the session you're trying to measure.

levels.explore: When the timer rings, hold up 1 to 5 fingers for how you feel, using the Mood check card.
levels.develop: Rate every 15 minutes for three sessions, and mark where the number dropped each time.
levels.extend: Compare the turn for two kinds of screen time, like a show and a game, and find out which one turns sooner.

steps.title: Pick one rule and predict
steps.why: A rule with a prediction is a test, not an order. Writing the prediction first is what makes the result count.
steps.kid: Your kid picks one rule from the Rule menu card, like devices charging outside bedrooms, screens only after time outside, or stopping at their turn. They write what they think will change, and by how much. Siblings can test different rules.
steps.you: Pick a rule for your own phone too, and write your prediction next to theirs. Kids notice whether grown-ups test themselves.
ask: What do you think will change?
How will we know if it worked?
steps.tip: One rule at a time. With two new rules in one week, nobody knows which one did the work.

levels.explore: Choose between two rules a parent reads out, and say if you think it will make you happier or grumpier.
levels.develop: Pick a rule, and write a prediction with a number in it, like falling asleep 10 minutes faster.
levels.extend: Before the week starts, write down what result would prove your prediction wrong.

steps.title: Run the test week
steps.why: A week is long enough to get past a grumpy first day, and short enough to stick to.
steps.kid: For a week, your kid lives with their rule and keeps the same notes every day, using the Test notes card: a mood number from 1 to 5 at the end of screen time, how easily they fell asleep, and one thing they made or did instead.
steps.you: Keep your own notes on your rule. Hold the rule steady all week, even on a hard day, so the test stays fair.
steps.tip: Don't judge the rule on day one. Look at the whole week before deciding anything.

levels.explore: Each evening, give the day a 1 to 5, and draw one thing you did instead of screens.
levels.develop: Keep all three notes every day, then hold the week up against your prediction.
levels.extend: At the end of the week, check the device report, work out how many minutes the rule saved, and find where those minutes went.

steps.title: Write the plan from the evidence
steps.why: Rules that came from their own results don't need to be enforced every day.
steps.kid: Your family lays out everyone's notes, keeps the rules that changed something and drops the ones that didn't, using the Plan from evidence card. Then you fill in Our screen plan at the end of the guide together, and everyone signs.
steps.you: Let the timer or the device settings do the stopping, so you don't have to. Put the check-in date on the calendar before anyone signs.
steps.tip: Before anyone signs, test-drive the full plan for three days with the timers on. A plan they've tried is easier to keep than one on paper.

levels.explore: Help choose one rule to keep, and set the timer with a parent.
levels.develop: Write your part of the plan with the result behind each rule, sign it and set the limits on the device.
levels.extend: Design the next experiment for the check-in: a rule nobody has tested yet, with your prediction already written.

skills.name: Testing

skills.name: Using evidence
skills.text: keeping only the rules that worked

skills.name: Self-control
skills.text: stopping when the plan says stop

conclusion.headline: Their screen rules came from their own results.
conclusion.text: Listen at the check-in for how they ask for a change. 'My notes showed I slept fine' instead of 'please, five more minutes' means they're arguing from evidence, and that kind of ask deserves a yes now and then.
conclusion.celebrate: When the timer goes off and they stop on their own, say: 'You tested that rule yourself, and now you're keeping it. That's your plan working.'
extensions: Swap roles for a day: the kids write a fair limit for a parent, and the parent tries it
Run the experiment again in six months, and see if the turn has moved
Test one rule on the whole family at once, like phones in a basket during meals, and compare everyone's notes
Keep the same three notes on a screen-free day, and compare it with an ordinary one

signs: They check the report before arguing about time
They notice when a session has turned
They ask for changes with a result, not a fuss
makeItReal: Tonight, have everyone write a guess for their daily screen time, grown-ups too, then open the reports together and read the real numbers out loud.

fromHome.text: We set each kid's screen limit together: they both said what would be fair and healthy for them, and we made a plan. When the time is up, the screen shuts down. They often ask for more, but they don't fuss when we say no.
